fix my morning routine.  Not tweak it.  Fix it.  Somewhere in the chaos of growing a business, managing responsibilities, and trying to keep all the moving pieces moving, my mornings had become unfocused.  I would get up, pour my coffee, open my computer, and immediately get pulled into whatever project was already on my mind.  One email turned into one task.  One task turned into one rabbit hole.  Before I knew it, I was rushing through my workout or cutting pieces of it short.  That is not me.  I am regimented. I love structure. I function best with a routine.  But even disciplined people can drift when life gets cluttered.  So I thought back to a time when my mornings felt focused, unrushed, and purposeful. It was right after I read *The Miracle Morning* by Hal Elrod.  The framework is S.A.V.E.R.S.:  **Silence** **Affirmation** **Visualization** **Exercise** **Reading** **Scribing**  Sixty minutes a day.  It does not have to happen in that exact order. For me, exercise comes at the end because I want space for a full workout, not a rushed version of one.  The point is not perfection.  The point is intention. I'm an avid Peloton user, and I love their training programs. Recently, I started the Progression Run program. Ironically, it's designed for beginner runners.  I'm not a beginner.  So why would I choose it?  Because I needed a reset. I wanted to return to the foundation. To slow down. To pay attention to form. To focus on breathing, cadence, pacing, and consistency instead of speed.  There were moments when the coach said, \"Recovery pace.\"  Every instinct told me I could go faster. But I didn't.  I trusted the process. I followed the coaching.  Because sometimes discipline isn't pushing harder. Sometimes discipline is resisting the urge to.  Leadership is no different.  As we gain experience, it's easy to believe we've outgrown the fundamentals. We stop listening as closely. We skip steps. We rely on what we've always done. But the best leaders I know never stop returning to the basics.  They sharpen their communication. They strengthen relationships. They revisit accountability. They seek feedback. They stay coachable.  You don't build excellence by constantly chasing the next advanced technique. You build it by mastering the fundamentals over and over again. Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Highlights cross-functional breakdowns","caption":"Friday Field Note: Patients often judge the experience at the transition points. The handoff from call center to clinic. The move from waiting room to exam room. The shift from visit to follow-up. The moment after a test result. The discharge instruction that determines confidence at home. Transitions reveal whether the organization is coordinated. When transitions are unclear, patients feel the burden of the system. When transitions are designed well, patients feel guided. A culture of care pays attention to these moments because they are where trust can either strengthen or weaken quickly. The experience is rarely one moment. It is the connection between moments.","cta":"Choose one transition point and ask patients and staff what feels unclear.","visual":"Patient journey line with transition moments highlighted","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #CareCoordination"},{"n":15,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Practical fix for uncertainty and perceived wait","caption":"The Friday Fix: Create a start-of-visit expectation standard. At the beginning of the encounter, patients should know three things: What will happen today. Who they will interact with. What should happen after the visit. This does not require a long script. It requires consistency. When expectations are clear, patients feel more oriented and staff spend less time answering preventable questions later. A culture of care is built through small moments of clarity repeated reliably. This week, ask: Do patients know what to expect before they have to ask?","cta":"Test this standard with one department or clinic team next week.","visual":"Three-part expectation card: Today, Team, Next Step","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientEngagement"},{"n":16,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Connects patient confidence to workflow reliability","caption":"What good looks like: discharge with confidence. A patient should not leave wondering what to do next, who to call, or what warning signs matter. A strong discharge experience is clear, teachable, and supported by follow-up. The team confirms understanding, avoids unnecessary jargon, and makes the next step visible. The patient leaves with confidence. The staff leave knowing the message was understood. This is not only a communication issue. It is a workflow issue. A culture of care ensures the final moments of an encounter are not rushed, confusing, or dependent on memory alone.","cta":"Review one discharge or after-visit process through the patient’s eyes.","visual":"Discharge checklist with confidence cues","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #DischargePlanning"},{"n":17,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Questions incentive and performance alignment","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: Is your culture rewarding speed over care? Healthcare teams are under pressure to move quickly. But when speed becomes the only visible priority, patients may experience rushed communication and staff may feel forced to choose between compassion and throughput. The goal is not to slow the system down. The goal is to design a system where efficiency and care can coexist. Leaders shape culture by what they measure, coach, praise, and tolerate. Ask this week: Are our operational expectations helping staff deliver care well, or forcing them to recover after the process fails?","cta":"Use this question in your next manager meeting.","visual":"Balance scale: Efficiency and Care","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #HealthcareLeadership"},{"n":18,"type":"Friday Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Links culture, burnout, and workflow design","caption":"Friday Field Note: Rework has a culture cost. When staff spend the day correcting missing information, chasing answers, repeating instructions, or explaining process breakdowns, empathy becomes harder to sustain. This does not mean staff do not care. It means the system is draining capacity that should be available for care. A culture of care must protect both patients and the people serving them. Workflow improvement is not only about efficiency. It is about reducing unnecessary friction so teams can bring more presence, patience, and compassion to the moments that matter. Operational design is emotional design.","cta":"Identify one source of avoidable rework that affects both patients and staff.","visual":"Rework loop showing staff capacity drain","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #EmployeeExperience"},{"n":19,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Offers a simple way to find communication gaps","caption":"The Friday Fix: Track the questions patients ask repeatedly. For one week, ask front-line teams to capture the top five questions they answer over and over. Then ask: Where should this information have been clearer? Which questions point to unclear instructions? Which questions point to process uncertainty? Which questions create avoidable call volume or front-desk pressure? Repeated questions are not interruptions. They are signals. They show where the patient journey needs better communication, better timing, or better design. When the process answers predictable questions early, everyone benefits.","cta":"Start with one team and collect repeated questions for five business days.","visual":"Top 5 patient questions tracker","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientCommunication"},{"n":20,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Frames operations as the infrastructure of care","caption":"What good looks like: compassionate workflows. A compassionate workflow makes the right thing easier to do. It helps staff anticipate needs, communicate clearly, reduce patient effort, and recover quickly when something goes wrong. It does not rely on memory, personality, or heroic effort. It creates reliable conditions for care. In healthcare, compassion is often described as a behavior. It is also an operating principle. When the workflow supports the behavior, the culture becomes more consistent. That is why patient experience improvement cannot be separated from operational improvement. The experience lives inside the workflow.","cta":"Use this language when connecting culture work to process improvement.","visual":"Workflow as the foundation under compassionate behaviors","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #CultureTransformation"},{"n":21,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Encourages metric and accountability review","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: Are your metrics driving the behavior you actually want? A metric can focus attention. It can also narrow attention. If teams are measured only on speed, they may rush. If they are measured only on satisfaction, they may avoid hard conversations. If they are measured without context, they may disengage. Patient experience measurement should lead to learning, not blame. The leadership opportunity is to connect metrics to behaviors, workflows, and coaching. Ask: What do our measures encourage our teams to do every day? That answer matters to culture.","cta":"Review one patient experience metric and identify the behavior it is currently shaping.","visual":"Metric → Behavior → Experience chain","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #HealthcareMetrics"},{"n":22,"type":"Friday Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Connects communication to trust and emotional experience","caption":"Friday Field Note: Silence creates anxiety. When patients do not know what is happening, when they will be seen, who is responsible, or what comes next, they begin filling in the gaps themselves. That uncertainty can make even a reasonable delay feel careless. A culture of care does not wait for patients to become frustrated before communicating. It builds proactive communication into the workflow. The message does not need to be complex. It needs to be timely, honest, and respectful. In many cases, the experience improves not because the wait disappeared, but because uncertainty did.","cta":"Identify one point where proactive communication could reduce patient anxiety.","visual":"Silence vs. clarity comparison card","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientTrust"},{"n":23,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Concrete process standard for a common pain point","caption":"The Friday Fix: Create a delay communication standard. Choose one setting where delays happen often. Define: When patients should be updated. Who is responsible for the update. What information should be shared. What options, if any, should be offered. How staff should escalate when the delay worsens. This is not scripting for the sake of scripting. It is consistency for the sake of trust. Patients should not have to ask to be informed. A culture of care anticipates predictable frustration and responds before it becomes a complaint.","cta":"Pilot this standard in one high-delay area for two weeks.","visual":"Delay communication standard template","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #ClinicFlow"},{"n":24,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Distinguishes rounding from visibility theater","caption":"What good looks like: leadership rounding that leads to improvement. Effective rounding is not only asking, “How is everything going?” It is listening for barriers, validating what teams experience, and closing the loop on what will change. Staff need to see that speaking up leads to action. Patients need to feel that leaders understand the real experience of care. A strong rounding process captures themes, assigns follow-up, and reports back. That is how rounding becomes more than visibility. It becomes a tool for culture, accountability, and operational learning. Care improves when leaders stay close to the work.","cta":"Add a close-the-loop step to your next rounding process.","visual":"Rounding loop: Listen → Capture → Act → Report back","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #LeadershipRounding"},{"n":25,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Invites leaders to examine psychological safety and process reliability","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: Do frontline teams trust the escalation process? When staff know how to escalate and believe leadership will respond, small issues are less likely to become patient experience failures. When escalation feels unclear, slow, or punitive, staff often create workarounds or absorb the problem themselves. A culture of care depends on psychological safety and operational clarity. Ask your teams: When something is getting in the way of patient care, do you know exactly what to do next? Then ask the harder question: Do you believe the response will help?","cta":"Use these two questions in your next frontline listening session.","visual":"Escalation confidence scale","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PsychologicalSafety"},{"n":26,"type":"Score Behind the Score","theme":"HMCG - Client Lesson / Trend / Myth vs. Reality","note":"Moves prospects from measurement to consulting diagnosis","caption":"Score Behind the Score: The number is not the whole story. Patient experience scores can point leaders in the right direction, but they rarely explain the full cause. A low score may reflect communication, access, handoffs, expectations, staffing pressure, unclear accountability, or workflow friction. The score is the signal. The real work is diagnosis. Before moving directly to training, scripting, or reminders, ask: What is the experience behind the score? What workflow produced it? What support do staff need to change it reliably? Improvement starts when measurement becomes learning.","cta":"Use this lens before designing your next patient experience action plan.","visual":"Score → Signal → Diagnosis → Improvement pathway","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientExperienceStrategy"},{"n":27,"type":"Friday Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Expands patient experience beyond the visit","caption":"Friday Field Note: The patient experience starts before the patient arrives. It starts with the phone call, the portal message, the referral process, the instructions, the reminder, and the question of whether the patient knows what to do next. By the time someone reaches the front desk, they may already feel confident or frustrated. Access is not only an appointment slot. It is the ease, clarity, and reliability of getting to care. A culture of care pays attention to the pre-visit experience because it sets expectations before the clinical encounter begins. The visit does not start at check-in. It starts at first contact.","cta":"Review your pre-visit experience as part of your patient journey work.","visual":"Pre-visit journey timeline","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #AccessExperience"},{"n":28,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Tactical action for leadership visibility","caption":"The Friday Fix: Call your own phone line. Use a common patient scenario and test the experience. How long does it take to reach the right person? Are the options clear? What happens after hours? Can the patient resolve their need without being transferred repeatedly? Does the portal message create clarity or more work? Digital and phone access are often treated as separate from patient experience, but patients do not separate them. They experience one organization. This week, test one access path and document what the patient must figure out alone.","cta":"Ask one leader to complete this test and share the findings with the team.","visual":"Access test scorecard","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #DigitalHealth"},{"n":29,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Defines a clear operational win","caption":"What good looks like: first-contact resolution. When patients reach out, the best experience is not being politely transferred five times. It is being guided clearly, resolved efficiently, or connected to the right next step with context intact. First-contact resolution requires more than friendly service. It requires information access, clear decision rights, training, workflow design, and escalation pathways. The patient experiences competence. The staff experience clarity. A culture of care removes unnecessary loops. When the first contact is reliable, trust begins earlier and frustration is reduced before the patient ever walks through the door.","cta":"Assess whether your teams have the information and authority to resolve common requests.","visual":"First-contact resolution flow","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #OperationalEfficiency"},{"n":30,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Creates empathy and process awareness","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: What are patients expected to figure out alone? How to schedule. Where to park. What to bring. Which portal message matters. What the next step is. Who to call after the visit. Whether a delay is normal. What a bill means. Every unanswered question adds effort. A culture of care reduces avoidable effort by making the next step clear. Leaders can start by identifying where the organization assumes knowledge patients may not have. The experience improves when the system stops making patients translate the process for themselves.","cta":"Ask a patient advisory group or frontline team to identify the top unclear moments.","visual":"List graphic: Things patients should not have to figure out alone","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #PatientCenteredCare"},{"n":31,"type":"Friday Field Note","theme":"HMCG - Friday Field Note","note":"Moves culture from slogan to observable behavior","caption":"Friday Field Note: Culture is revealed under pressure. It is easy to describe care values when the schedule is on time, staffing is stable, and patients are calm. The real test is what happens when the day is behind, the waiting room is full, the phones are heavy, and the team is stretched. Do expectations stay clear? Do leaders support the team? Do patients still receive respectful communication? Do staff feel safe raising concerns? A culture of care is not proven by the words on the wall. It is proven by the behaviors the organization protects when pressure rises.","cta":"Observe one high-pressure period and note what the culture rewards.","visual":"Culture under pressure thermometer","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #WorkplaceCulture"},{"n":32,"type":"The Friday Fix","theme":"HMCG - The Friday Fix","note":"Turns values into measurable behaviors","caption":"The Friday Fix: Define one care value in operational terms. Choose a value your organization uses often, such as respect, compassion, teamwork, or accountability. Then answer: What does this look like in patient communication? What does it look like during a delay? What does it look like in a handoff? What does it look like when a staff member needs help? What does it look like when expectations are missed? Values become culture when people know what they mean in daily work. This week, translate one value into observable behaviors.","cta":"Use this exercise with managers during your next culture discussion.","visual":"Value-to-behavior translation worksheet","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #CultureOfCare"},{"n":33,"type":"What Good Looks Like","theme":"HMCG - What Great Looks Like","note":"Supports culture-building and leadership trust","caption":"What good looks like: accountability without blame. A strong culture of care does not avoid accountability. It makes accountability constructive. The question is not, “Who failed?” The better questions are: Was the expectation clear? Was the workflow realistic? Was the team trained and supported? Did leadership follow through? What needs to change so the right action becomes easier next time? Blame shuts down learning. Accountability strengthens learning. Healthcare teams need standards, coaching, and systems that make consistent care possible. That is how accountability becomes a culture builder instead of a fear trigger.","cta":"Use these questions when reviewing a patient experience miss.","visual":"Accountability questions framework","tags":"#PatientExperience #HealthcareLeadership #CultureOfCare #HealthcareOperations #JustCulture"},{"n":34,"type":"Leadership Reflection","theme":"HMCG - Leadership Reflection","note":"Targets operational constraint behind culture inconsistency","caption":"Friday Leadership Reflection: Do your managers have time to coach the culture you want? Many organizations ask managers to improve patient experience, support staff, monitor metrics, resolve issues, and keep operations moving.
